notes.meaning: Job contrasts his past honor with his present humiliation. Men younger than him now laugh at him, though their fathers were so unreliable that Job would not have trusted them to guard his sheepdogs. In ancient times, younger people were expected to treat their elders with deep respect, so this mockery stung him sharply.

Job explains why those fathers were of no help to him in earlier days. They were weak and lazy, and poor living had drained away whatever strength they ever had. They were useless in their youth and reached old age with neither strength nor wisdom.

These families were starved, gaunt, and desperate, roaming the barren desert for anything to eat. They chewed on whatever dry roots and plants they could find in the wasteland by night. Their shameful poverty kept them far away from civilized towns.

Driven by severe hunger, they picked salty wild leaves among the desert bushes and dug up the bitter roots of the broom tree for food. These harsh desert plants were barely edible and offered almost no nutrition. Only the most desperate outcasts resorted to eating them.

Townspeople drove these vagrants away because they were seen as dishonest and dangerous. Whenever they showed their faces near villages, people shouted after them to chase them off as if they were thieves. They were completely shut out from normal human society.

Because they were banished from towns, they had to shelter in deep ravines, rocky cliffs, and holes in the ground. They lived like outcasts in the roughest wilderness, hiding away from sight in fear and shame.
Out in the brush, they cried out and groaned like wild donkeys starving for food. They huddled together under thorn bushes and stinging nettles to seek shelter and keep warm.

Job describes them as a foolish, nameless crowd who had been beaten and driven out of the country. They came from families of no reputation, and they had none themselves. Job mentions their low standing to show how deep his own disgrace had become, since even the lowest outcasts felt free to despise him.
Now the children of those very outcasts make up taunting songs about Job. He has become a common joke and a byword, an object of gossip and ridicule among the lowest people around.

These mockers keep their distance because they are disgusted by Job's sores, yet they do not hesitate to spit toward him to show their contempt. Spitting in front of someone or in their face was one of the worst insults known in the ancient world. Many Christian readers see a reminder here of Jesus, who was also despised and spat upon by crowds.

God had taken away Job's power and honor, unstringing his bow and leaving him defenseless. Because God had brought him low, these rude youths no longer felt any fear or restraint, and they attacked him openly.

A disrespectful mob crowds in on Job's right side, the very place an accuser would take in a court of law. They push him off balance and prepare to overwhelm him, just as soldiers build dirt ramps against a city wall to destroy it.
They tear up Job's path to cut off any way for him to find help or escape. They take pleasure in piling on more misery, and no one steps forward to hold them back.
His tormentors rush upon him like enemy soldiers bursting through a broken section of a city wall. They tumble in like a sudden flood when a dam breaks, rolling over Job and leaving him ruined.

Sudden terrors sweep over Job from every direction, driving away his dignity as quickly as a gust of wind. The good days and prosperity he once enjoyed have completely vanished, passing by like a morning cloud.
Job feels his life and strength melting away inside him in floods of tears and sorrow. Painful days of suffering have grabbed hold of him like a trap, and he cannot break free.
Even at night, when other people find sleep and relief, Job's pain never stops. Deep, throbbing aches pierce all the way into his bones, and his gnawing sores give him no rest at all.

The terrible disease clings to Job's body and ruins his clothes, sticking tightly to his open sores like the tight neck of a shirt. His sick, crusty skin wraps around him like an inescapable garment of suffering.
Job feels as though God Himself has thrown him down into the dirt and mud. He feels completely worthless, brought down to the level of dust and ashes.
Job calls out to God for rescue, but God remains silent and gives no answer. Even when Job stands up and keeps praying, God seems only to stare at him without offering any help or comfort.
In the middle of his intense grief, Job feels that God has turned harsh and severe toward him. Instead of protecting him, God's mighty hand seems to be attacking him like an enemy.
Job compares his helplessness to being lifted up by a violent whirlwind and tossed around like dry straw or chaff. The gale of trouble beats against him and dissolves all his strength.
Job feels sure that his sickness will soon end in death. He recognizes that the grave is the final meeting place God has appointed for every living person.

A person falling into ruin naturally cries out and reaches for help in their misery. Job also takes comfort in the thought that God's severe hand will not keep striking him once he is resting safely in the grave.
Job remembers how tenderly he cared for others when they were suffering. He had wept with those who were having hard days, and his heart had ached for the poor and helpless.

Because Job had treated others with mercy, he hoped and expected that peace and blessings would continue in his own life. Instead, crushing disaster overtook him, and deep darkness fell right where he had looked for light.
Job suffers deep churning inside, both from the burning heat of fever and from intense emotional grief. Days of misery overtook him without warning, shattering all his plans for a quiet life.
Job wanders around blackened by painful disease, not from sitting in the sun. In his desperate agony, he stands up before the public assembly to weep and plead for help.
Job feels like a close brother to jackals and ostriches that live in lonely desert ruins. His nonstop groans and cries sound just like the eerie, mournful wailing of those wild animals.
His skin has turned dark and peels away from his sores because of his severe illness. A raging fever burns deep inside him, drying out his bones and strength.
The musical instruments that once filled Job's home with joy and celebration now produce only sad sounds. His harp and flute have been tuned to the bitter cries of mourning and weeping.
